chapter.title: The oorexx Module: Python Using Rexx
chapter.para: A Python program uses Rexx through the module oorexx: import oorexx. It creates interpreter instances, runs Rexx code in them, and uses Rexx objects as Python objects. The module is the bridge itself, the same binary for every Python from 3.9 on.

Its names are Python's, and its methods' names follow Python's conventions (add_command_environment), but for the sendMessage methods of RexxObject, which keep the names of BSF4ooRexx's RexxProxy. The syntax diagrams of this chapter show Python syntax.

section.title: Interpreter Class
section.para: An ooRexx interpreter instance. A process may have several at once, each with its own .local, packages and ADDRESS environments. An instance loads python.cls by itself, so the Rexx code it runs can use &py; without requiring it. It is a context manager: the end of a with block closes it.

section.title: Interpreter
section.para: Creates an interpreter instance. The keyword arguments are ooRexx's instance options, and the bridge's:

listitem.para: a directory, or a list of them, where CALL, ::requires and run look for programs.
a file extension, or a list of them, tried for external calls.
a native library, or a list of them, loaded when the instance is created.
a dict from names to Python callables: ADDRESS environments ().
True (the default) sends Rexx's standard streams through Python's; False keeps Rexx's own ().
True (the default), False, or a dict of prefixes for Rexx's lines ().

section.title: run
section.para: CALLs the Rexx program program, a file name, with the arguments, and returns its result (&None; if it returns none). The arguments and the result follow .

section.title: eval
section.para: Returns the value of the Rexx expression.

section.title: routine
section.para: Returns a Rexx routine made from source (clauses separated by semicolons or line feeds), named name (default ROUTINE). It is a RexxObject, and a Python callable: calling it calls the routine with the arguments, and returns its result.

example.title: Interpreter: eval, routine, run
example.programlisting:
import oorexx
with open("add.rex", "w") as f: f.write("use arg a, b; return a + b\n") with oorexx.Interpreter(rexx_path=".") as rexx: print(rexx.eval("2 ** 10"), rexx.eval("reverse('abc')")) double = rexx.routine("use arg x; return x * 2") print(double(21), double("21")) print(rexx.run("add.rex", 2, 3))

section.title: add_command_environment
section.para: Makes the Python callable handler the ADDRESS environment name (), at any time, from any thread ().

section.title: remove_command_environment
section.para: Makes the ADDRESS environment name, written in Python, unknown again: a command sent to it is then FAILURE with RC 30, as ooRexx answers for an environment it does not know (ooRexx has no way to remove an environment: the bridge forgets the name). A name that is not an environment written in Python is a ValueError; other environments are not touched. Returns &None;.

section.title: close
section.para: Terminates the interpreter instance. Using it afterwards raises RexxError.

section.title: RexxObject Class
section.para: A Rexx object, by reference, as BSF4ooRexx's RexxProxy is in Java. It keeps the Rexx object alive while Python holds it. Rexx strings, numbers, &nil; and Arrays do not come as RexxObjects, but converted ().

table.title: Python on a RexxObject, and the Rexx message it sends

row.entry: o~name(a, b): the attribute's name, uppercased
o~call(a, b): a Routine is called
the same Rexx object; equal objects have the same hash, so a RexxObject can be a dict key

section.para: An attribute of a RexxObject, o.name, is a callable oorexx.RexxMessage, which sends the message when it is called: o.name() sends NAME with no arguments. Two RexxObjects of the same Rexx object are ==, though not is; a RexxObject given back to Rexx is the Rexx object itself.

example.title: Rexx objects in Python
example.programlisting:
import oorexx
with oorexx.Interpreter() as rexx: d = rexx.eval(".directory~new") d["X"] = 1 d["Y"] = 2 print(len(d), d["X"], d.hasIndex("Y"), sorted(d), str(d)) print(d.items(), type(d.items).__name__) q = rexx.eval(".queue~new") q.queue("a"); q.queue("b") print(q.pull(), q.items()) print(d == rexx.routine("use arg x; return x")(d))

section.title: sendMessage
section.para: Sends the message name, a string, with the arguments in a list, and returns the result. It reaches the messages that cannot be written as Python attributes ("[]=", "||"), and a name held in a variable.

section.title: sendMessage0 ... sendMessage5
section.para: Send the message name with no arguments, or with one to five, given one by one.

section.title: sendMessageScope
section.para: Sends the message name with the method search starting at the class scope (a RexxObject for a Rexx class), as Rexx's o~name:scope(args).

example.title: Messages by name
example.programlisting:
import oorexx
with oorexx.Interpreter() as rexx: d = rexx.eval(".directory~new") d.sendMessage("[]=", ["x", "K"]) # d["K"] = "x" print(d.sendMessage("[]", ["K"]), d.sendMessage0("ITEMS"), d.sendMessage1("HASINDEX", "K")) o = rexx.eval(".object~new") print(o.sendMessageScope("STRING", rexx.eval(".object")))

section.title: RexxError Class
section.para: The exception that a Rexx condition becomes in Python, a subclass of RuntimeError. Its text is Rexx's message, with the condition's code: Rexx error 42.3: Arithmetic overflow; divisor must not be zero. A Python exception that went through Rexx code is raised as itself instead ().
Its attributes are the parts of the Rexx condition, as Rexx's condition("O") has them:

listitem.para: the condition's name: "SYNTAX" for an error.
a SYNTAX condition's code, a str: "42.3".
an int: a SYNTAX condition's major number, 42.
the condition's message, the secondary one for an error.
the line where it was raised, an int.
the program where it was raised: a file name, or a routine's name.
the condition's description, if it has one.
the Rexx traceback, as Rexx shows it when the error is not trapped: its lines joined by line ends.

section.para: An attribute the condition does not have is &None;, and so are all of them when the error is not a Rexx condition (an interpreter that has been closed).

example.title: The parts of a Rexx condition
example.programlisting:
import oorexx
with oorexx.Interpreter() as rexx: divide = rexx.routine("say 'one'\nreturn 1 / 0", name="DIVIDE") try: divide() except oorexx.RexxError as e: print(e) print(e.condition, e.code, e.rc, e.position, e.program) print(e.errortext) print(e.traceback)
example.screen: REXXout>one Rexx error 42.3: Arithmetic overflow; divisor must not be zero. SYNTAX 42.3 42 2 DIVIDE Arithmetic overflow/underflow. 2 *-* return 1 / 0 *-* Compiled method "CALL" with scope "Routine".

section.title: ADDRESS Environments in Python
section.para: A Python callable can be a Rexx command environment: given with command_environments= when the interpreter is created, or with , or from Rexx with . Rexx's ADDRESS name commands call it with two arguments, the command, a str, and a . What it returns is RC, whatever its sign; &None; is 0. It raises ERROR or FAILURE only through the context's and . A Python exception in the handler is a SYNTAX error (98.900) there, as any other (), and, if the Rexx code does not trap it, Python gets it back as itself. Without WITH, what the handler writes goes to Python's sys.stdout and sys.stderr. An environment belongs to its interpreter instance; adding a name again replaces it, and (or ) makes it unknown again.

example.title: ADDRESS environments written in Python
example.programlisting:
import oorexx
def calc(command, ctx): try: ctx.set_var("RESULT", eval(command, {"__builtins__": {}})) return 0 except Exception as e: ctx.set_var("RESULT", str(e)) return 1
def upper(command, ctx): for line in ctx.lines(): ctx.output(line.upper()) return 0
with oorexx.Interpreter(command_environments={"CALC": calc}, prefixes=False) as rexx: rexx.add_command_environment("UPPER", upper) rexx.routine(""" address calc '2 ** 10'; say rc result '1 / 0'; say rc result in.1 = 'one'; in.2 = 'two'; in.0 = 2 address upper 'x' with input stem in. output stem out. say out.0 out.1 out.2 """)()

section.title: CommandContext Class
section.para: What an ADDRESS environment written in Python gets with each command: the command's redirected input and output (ADDRESS ... WITH), the variables of the Rexx code that issued it, and the conditions to raise there. It is valid only during the call.

section.title: line_in
section.para: Returns the next line of the redirected input, or &None; at the end.

section.title: lines
section.para: Returns a list of all the lines of the redirected input.

section.title: output
section.para: Writes line to the command's output: the redirected output if there is one, else Python's sys.stdout, as a real command writes to the console.

section.title: error
section.para: Writes line to the command's error output: the redirected one if there is one, else Python's sys.stderr.

section.title: is_redirected
section.para: Returns whether the command's input, output or error is redirected, or, for 'same', whether output and error go to the same target.

section.title: get_var
section.para: Returns the value of the variable name of the code that issued the command, or &None; if it has none.

section.title: set_var
section.para: Sets the variable name of the code that issued the command.

section.title: drop_var
section.para: Drops the variable name of the code that issued the command.

section.title: raise_error
section.para: Raises ERROR in the code that issued the command, after the command, with RC rc (when the handler returns &None;, rc is RC); returns rc, so that it can be returned: return ctx.raise_error(5).

section.title: raise_failure
section.para: The same, raising FAILURE.
